newsitem.title: INDIA: India parties eye election as coalition cracks sho.
newsitem.headline: India parties eye election as coalition cracks sho.

text.p: India's political parties have begun preparing for a mid-term election after a split in Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's party that weakened his minority coalition, politicians and analysts said on Wednesday.
"Everybody is getting ready for elections," a cabinet minister in the 15-party United Front coalition, who did not want to be identified, told Reuters by telephone.
The United Front combines regional groups, centrist parties and communists.
Gujral's Janata Dal party was split last Saturday by its then president, Laloo Prasad Yadav, who formed a powerful breakaway group that has named itself the Rashtriya (Nationalist) Janata Dal (RJD).
The next day his rival, Sharad Yadav -- no relative of his -- was declared elected as Janata Dal president in polls held last Thursday.
Laloo Yadav, a popular low-caste leader mired in a corruption scandal, cited the alleged rigging of voter lists in the party poll as the reason for his ouster.

Despite the political turmoil, Gujral's two-month-old rule appeared secure. Laloo Yadav, chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, immediately pledged the support of his breakaway RJD to the prime minister.
The RJD has taken 18 of the Janta Dal's 45 deputies.
"It is a fairly critical period for the government," said analyst Mahesh Rangarajan at the Centre for Contemporary Studies. "Any one thing can upset the apple cart," he said.
But he added that there was no immediate threat to the government. "It is vulnerable but not yet fragile," he said.
Trouble erupted on Tuesday as leftist coalition partners said they wanted RJD out of the United Front if Laloo Yadav did not resign as chief minister and face trial for corruption.

Yadav has been indicted by federal police in a $280 million corruption scandal in which he is among 56 politicians and officials accused of embezzling animal welfare funds in Bihar. But he says he is innocent and has rejected calls from alliance partners to step down.

Gujral has refused to sack three federal government ministers who joined the breakaway RJD, but his Janata Dal colleagues will continue to try to persuade the premier to force out the party renegades.
"This will drag on," the cabinet minister said, and added: "If Laloo resigns, his group can stay in the government."
Leftist political parties led by the communists may quit the coalition if the RJD was allowed to stay on without Laloo Yadav resigning, the minister said.

But the crucial factor for the government is the Congress party. Congress offers the make-or-break support of its 140 lawmakers to the United Front, which has 178 deputies in the 545-member lower house, Lok Sabha, elected in April/May 1996.
Rangarajan said Laloo Yadav's close relations with Congress president Sitaram Kesri could help Gujral's government.

Congress backed the United Front in June 1996 to oust a 12-day-old government formed by its arch foe, the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janta Party (BJP), which is the largest group in parliament with 193 votes.

But Congress pulled its support in April and toppled the United Front government headed by then prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda, accusing him of failing to contain the BJP. The United Front changed leaders to win back Congress' support.
Rangarajan said Congress was expected to support Laloo Yadav's RJD, and thus Gujral.
Nevertheless, things would still not be smooth, he said. "I don't see a stable arrangement emerging in this house. There will certainly be a mid-term poll," he added.
